items.t: EOG Resources Q3 Earnings Call Highlights
sum: - Interested in EOG Resources, Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

- Record Q3 production and strong cash generation: EOG reported adjusted earnings of $4.87 per share and $2.2 billion in free cash flow, while maintaining its 2026 outlook for 5% oil production growth and $6.5 billion in capital spending.

- Higher dividend and shareholder returns: EOG raised its annual regular dividend by 8% to $4.40 per share and returned just over $1.5 billion to investors in Q3, primarily through dividends and share buybacks.

- Expanding gas infrastructure and sales: EOG signed a 10-year Gulf Coast gas supply agreement linked to JKM pricing and approved a roughly $300 million Janus plant expansion, expected to double processing capacity by the second half of 2028.
- SM Energy's Civitas Merger Is Paying Off, But the Stock's Run Raises the Bar

EOG Resources (NYSE:EOG) reported record oil, natural gas liquids and natural gas production in the third quarter of 2026 and raised its regular dividend by 8% for 2027, as executives outlined plans for modest oil growth and further investment in gas infrastructure.

The company earned an adjusted $4.87 per share and generated $2.2 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, Chief Financial Officer Ann Janssen said on the earnings call. Adjusted cash flow from operations was $7.23 per share.

Why Did EOG Resources (NYSE:EOG) Lift Its Tax Guidance Before Results?
sum: - A filing raised guidance for current tax expense to a noticeably higher range than before.
- The company attributed the change to crude prices that came in above its August assumptions amid the Middle East conflict.
- Full results and a webcast call are scheduled for Friday, with a Brent-linked gas contract set to begin deliveries in January.

EOG Resources (NYSE:EOG) Energy EOG Resources Inc (NYSE:EOG) 155.17 USD -2.720 1.723% Last Updated at: 2026-11-03T21:00:00Z rarely uses a regulatory filing to say much about the quarter before its results, which is why a short document submitted in early October drew notice. The news adds to the running story across Oil and Gas Stocks.

The reason, according to the filing, was straightforward: crude oil prices during the quarter came in higher than the company assumed when it last updated guidance, and the company expects higher prices to persist for the full year because of the Middle East conflict. EOG Resources counts as a member of the S&P 500, the NYSE Composite and the Russell 1000. A higher tax bill is, in effect, a by-product of higher taxable earnings, so the filing serves as an indirect hint about the strength of the period.

The document was a current report filed under the item used for results of operations and financial condition. In it, the company said it was updating guidance for current tax expense for the latest quarter.

Current tax expense is the portion of the corporate tax charge that is payable in the near term, as opposed to deferred tax, which reflects timing differences. When pre-tax earnings rise because commodity prices are higher, the amount payable currently rises in step, particularly for a company that is generating more cash than it spends on drilling and can therefore not defer as much through deductions.

Oil Producers Slide as Crude Retreats: EOG Resources Drops 6%, ConocoPhillips and Occidental Petroleum Fall 5%
sum: Crude prices retreated Wednesday and the pain landed squarely on exploration and production names, skipping refiners and midstream entirely. Here is why that mechanical link turned a commodity move into a sector-wide shakeout for some of the biggest names in…

Oil and gas producers are sliding Wednesday morning as crude oil prices retreat, dragging exploration and production names lower across the board. The move is concentrated in the energy patch rather than the tape. The SPDR S&P Oil & Gas Exploration & Production ETF (NYSEARCA:XOP) is down 4% to $192.43, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.4% to $760.45.

ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP | COP Price Prediction) stock is down 5% to $134.29, giving back part of a recent advance. Meanwhile, EOG Resources (NYSE:EOG) shares are falling 6% to $145.16, leading the three featured names lower. Occidental Petroleum (NYSE:OXY) stock is sliding 5% to $60.16, tracking the same commodity pressure.

ConocoPhillips, EOG Resources, and Occidental Petroleum are exploration and production companies that own the barrels they sell, so a fall in the crude price passes into their realized prices directly. That mechanical link is the whole of today’s story, with no company-specific news bridging the three. Each of the three producers is down by more than XOP, which puts the sharpest pain at the pure-play end of the group.

Owning producing acreage rather than refining margins or midstream fees means ConocoPhillips, EOG Resources, and Occidental Petroleum see revenue swing with the crude price rather than against it. Such commodity leverage cuts both ways. It has cut in favor of the group for stretches this year before turning against them on this session.

The absence of individual catalysts across ConocoPhillips, EOG Resources, and Occidental Petroleum is itself the tell. When three producers with different basins, hedging profiles, and capital return programs all fall together on the same session, the driver sits above them at the commodity level rather than in any one boardroom. XOP’s decline confirms the pressure is sector-wide across E&P, not a rerating of one management team.

5 Best Oil Dividend Stocks for 2026 and How to Invest
sum: For investors prospecting the market for oil dividend stocks, deciding among the dozens of energy stocks that are also dividend stocks can be daunting. Making a sound choice can help investors sit back and enjoy watching their portfolios become energized by a steady stream of passive income.

Although oil stocks have often been a profitable choice for investors, rising calls for the adoption of renewable energy may suggest that oil companies -- and oil stocks -- will soon be in decline. A more likely scenario is that companies involved in oil production will continue to play a significant role, especially since petroleum is found in a variety of agricultural, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic products.

In the near term, the market is expected to continue growing. The International Energy Agency (IEA), for example, projects that global oil demand will increase by 2.5 million barrels per day between 2024 and 2030, reaching about 105.5 million barrels per day.
There are many options available to investors, but there's no need to burn the midnight oil looking for the most compelling choices. Let's take a look at five of the best.
Chevron stock is a common option for income investors as the company is one of the world's largest oil companies, with integrated operations spanning multiple aspects of the industry.

The company forecasts production growth at a 6% compound annual rate from 2024 through 2026, assuming Brent crude averages $70 per barrel. This should drive increasing free cash flow (FCF), with Permian assets alone projected to add about $2 billion in FCF by 2026. Management expects this growth to boost profitability, targeting a more than 3% improvement in return on capital employed (ROCE) by 2030 -- up from 7.2% in 2025 -- at the same $70 Brent assumption.

Traded on the New York Stock Exchange for over a century, Chevron is now the only energy stock in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The company has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years, and management expects to continue increasing shareholder distributions over the next five years if Brent crude stays above $50 per barrel.

3 Energy Stocks With Dividends That Have Never Been Cut
sum: Do you need reliable investment income for the indefinite future? Dividend stocks remain your best bet, particularly if you want this income to at least keep up with inflation. But some of the market's best dividend stocks come from a surprising industry... the energy sector. Despite all the wild ups and downs of oil (and natural gas) prices over the years, three energy stocks have never been forced to cut their dividend payments.

Oil giant Chevron (CVX -1.86%) has been through several changes in its long history, including being bought by Standard Oil, and its own acquisition of Gulf Oil in 1984. Its long-term dividend history is difficult to track, and doesn't mean much anyway.

We can say, however, that the Chevron we know and love today has been able to at least maintain its dividend payment for more than 50 years, overcoming many volatile price swings of crude oil that can work for and against its important upstream (exploring and drilling) business.

What Chevron has done to handle these swings without jeopardizing its ability to sustain its dividends is as obvious as it is simple. That is, it doesn't overcommit to these payments. Last year was a relatively lousy one for the industry, undermined by poor prices. Yet, Chevron's total 2025 per-share payout of $6.84 was still more than covered by last year's earnings.

Indeed, Chevron's not only paid a quarterly dividend like clockwork for decades, it has now raised its annual per-share payout for 39 consecutive years. Its current forward-looking dividend yield of 3.8% is also one of the best in the business at this time.

While Chevron manages an upstream (drilling) and downstream (refining) business, Enbridge (ENB -1.37%) operates in the middle. It's a midstream name, delivering gas and oil through its 18,000 miles of liquid pipelines and nearly 19,000 miles of natural gas pipelines in Canada and the United States. In fact, this company handles nearly one-third of all of North America's crude oil.

It's an ideal business model for supporting reliable dividends, too. The ever-changing prices of oil or gas don't affect its profitability, since the company simply charges a flat volume-based fee for the use of its pipeline network.

Big Gas Polluter Crowns EOG Resources as the Polluter of the Month for July 2026
sum: Original art by artist Deanne Chuck accompanies the polluter-of-the-month announcement.

Today, Big Gas Polluters announced EOG Resources as its July 2026 Polluter of the Month for walking back its methane reduction goals and having pollution events so large they’ve been spotted from space, all while actively working against climate action.

“We were surprised to find so many recent super-emitter events near EOG facilities,” said Geoff Bromaghim, Gas Leaks’ Director of Methane Accountability. “Large, sophisticated companies, such as EOG Resources, should be outperforming their peers when it comes to methane emissions. If the producer is serious about helping reduce emissions, they must start doing more.”

EOG Resources is one of the largest oil and gas producers in the United States and, in a past sustainability report, stated its intention “to reach net zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions by 2040.” While it has continued reinforcing its “commitment to leading environmental performance”, the Big Gas Polluter’s coalition found evidence that the company abandoned this goal in the past year.

Since the start of 2025, the coalition has also identified 23 super-emitter events emanating from 17 sources near EOG facilities in Texas and New Mexico by using observational data documented in Carbon Mapper’s public portal. The Environmental Protection Agency defines super-emitter events as incidents that release methane at a rate of at least 100 kilograms per hour. The most recent plumes include:
